How AI is changing software jobs

Over the past two years, companies across the technology sector have reported significant changes in how software teams are staffed. A survey of 1,200 engineering managers found that 38 percent had reduced hiring for junior developer roles, citing productivity gains from AI coding assistants as one of the main reasons.

At the same time, demand for engineers with experience in machine learning infrastructure grew sharply. Recruiters describe a market that is splitting in two: routine implementation work is increasingly automated, while roles that combine domain knowledge with system design remain hard to fill.

Economists caution that it is too early to attribute job losses directly to AI. Interest rates, post-pandemic over-hiring and a slowdown in venture funding all played a part in the layoffs of 2023 and 2024. Separating these effects requires longitudinal data that most surveys do not yet have.

Healthcare tells a different story. Hospitals that adopted AI documentation tools report that clinicians spend less time on paperwork, but staffing levels have not fallen; if anything, administrative roles have shifted toward supervising and correcting automated output.
